text: This is Resurrect, built today at the A-I-E Code Summit hackathon. It rebuilds old software from a short screen recording, and the builder never sees the original app. Then it proves the new version behaves the same. Fetch.ai is how you drive it: one agent on Agentverse that you talk to from A-S-I One.

Here is the whole pipeline. Claude watches the recording and writes down the rules. Those rules cross a wall into a clean room, where Claude Code builds the new app. A verifier replays the recording against the rebuild and scores it. Our Fetch.ai agent wraps all of it behind the Agent Chat Protocol.
The input is six seconds of a real 2018 medical billing app, Open E-M-R five, checking a claim for errors. Nothing else from the old app is ever handed to the builder.

From that recording Claude found thirty-two rules. Twenty-four it saw happen. Eight it's guessing, and it says so. For example: when the patient isn't the insurance holder, the patient's own birth date, sex and address must be filled in. That one was a guess.

Every handoff into the clean room is linted and logged with a hash: the exact prompt, every input file, every output. The builder runs as its own isolated Claude Code session, with no shell, no web, and no read access to the repo. Judges can audit the whole trail in wall dot log.

This is the rebuild. Its own look, built from the rule list only. It reproduces all twenty-two lines of the original error log. And when we switch the claim to a child on a parent's plan, a case it never saw in the recording, the patient checks fire.

Every score is checked against the real old app, which we ran with new data during the event. Runs one and two scored zero of four on hidden tests: a perfect replay of the recording taught it nothing. So the verifier started sending back the old app's behavior on two practice cases, while the four test cases stayed sealed. From run three on, it passes three of four.

Now the Fetch.ai part. The verifier is a micro-agent with a mailbox on Agentverse and the Agent Chat Protocol. It answers in plain language. Say hi for an introduction, rebuild for the story of the best saved run, or rebuild live to have Claude Code build a brand-new version on the spot.
Here it is in A-S-I One. One message tells the story: what was seen, what crossed the wall, and the score, with a link to try the new app. Then an interactive card asks a human to decide.

Rebuild live really runs the loop. The agent acknowledges in about two seconds, posts the rules and the handoff, and about two minutes later, Claude Code has built run five, the verifier has scored it, and the result comes back in the same conversation.

The one hidden test it misses is a bug in the old app: it accepts the letters A through J as a doctor's ID number. The new app requires digits. Resurrect doesn't decide that on its own. A person taps copy old or keep fix, and the decision is written to the same public log.
Record it. Resurrect rebuilds it, with proof. The code, the scores and the full log are on GitHub, and the agent is live on Agentverse. Just mention at-resurrect in A-S-I One.
